name: Beth Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach flute on Wednesdays, record short advert lines and play the community orchestra when my name is on the rota. I finished secondary school and still need the senior player’s help on some quick passages.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you at it, and what is hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a child finds enough breath to finish a phrase. I dislike not knowing whether the orchestra needs me next month when the family has already made plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the studio that an AI booking reply is useful if it gets the pupil into the right room. I would still teach the flute lesson and check the child’s breathing myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We have eight months of expenses saved and my partner has regular electrician work. I am junior on the community orchestra rota, but one missed concert does not upset the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep the Wednesday flute pupils and the orchestra’s weekend concerts this season. I already use AI daily to draft practice notes, and I check every fingering before sending them home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this picture. The family can absorb an ordinary cancelled date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when weather changed a concert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last concert moved indoors after rain and the fee held. I would ask the organiser to keep that weather clause next year, because it kept everyone from arguing at the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your daughter use in a lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter practises a short tune while I cook. A practice note cannot show my daughter where to breathe.

I would keep **live flute lessons** and concert dates.
think: Our **eight-month reserve** and electrician income protect the mortgage from one missed concert.
I still need to improve my **orchestra playing** to keep the rota.
do: Keep **Wednesday flute pupils** and weekend orchestra dates this season.
Check **AI practice notes** for fingerings before sending them home.
feel: I feel **calm** because the family can absorb one cancelled date.
S0.quote: A practice note cannot show my daughter where to breathe.
fieldNote: Her **eight-month cushion** and partner’s regular trade work make one missed concert manageable.
Her daily **AI use** is existing and checked against her own playing.

steps.text: Keep Wednesday flute pupils and weekend community orchestra dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the studio that AI may book pupils, write practice notes and make cheap backing tracks, so we should show what live lessons do. I would ask the manager for a written term of paid teaching hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My short flute recordings for local adverts could shrink by about one fifth of a busy month. The orchestra might use fewer players for small events too, though I do not know that yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would bring three months of lesson attendance to the studio manager and ask for the next paid term. In the first year I would trial a new AI note-checker only after a senior tutor demonstrates it on a nameless score, then play every suggested fingering and stop if one is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing my recording fees. Eight months saved gives us time. A smaller income still changes family plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would keep the note-checker safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not put pupil names or recordings into a tool that sends them outside the studio. If a trial cannot keep that boundary, I would use my own pencil notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the family postpone first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The advert recordings pay for the weekend trip when bookings are full. Losing a fifth of my advert recording income would postpone our family trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the studio that AGI by 2028 could write every exercise and advert track, but a child still needs a person hearing the breath. I would ask for a decision on paid lessons before the new term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the advert recordings to vanish in 2028 and some parents may test automated lessons. Robots for hands-on playing arrive around 2031. The flute studio could buy automated lessons before a robot ever plays a flute.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would ask the manager for a written lesson timetable and collect my last six recording invoices. If 2028 AGI cuts paid studio hours, I would apply for an advertised paid flute tutor post only if it accepts my secondary education and fits school pickup; I would keep pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about the recording loss and possible studio cuts, but eight months saved and nearby posts give us a route. I would not pretend the loss is harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the nearby tutor post actually open to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A nearby music school posted a part-time opening, but I have to check its qualification line. I will not spend a child’s pickup hour on an interview for a job I cannot hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner that the mortgage can be covered during a search. We would protect six months of expenses and cut the weekend trip before spending below it.

say: I would ask for a **written lesson timetable** before the new term.
I would defend **human breath coaching** for beginners.
think: My **advert recordings** likely end in 2028 before 2031 playing robots.
Parents may choose **automated lessons**, putting studio hours at risk.
do: Ask for a **written studio timetable** this week with six recording invoices.
Apply for an **advertised paid tutor post** after 2028 cuts only if qualified and pickup fits.

feel: I feel **anxious** about lost recordings, with a reserve for a search.
S2.quote: The flute studio could buy automated lessons before a robot ever plays a flute.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 thinking losses** from the later 2031 robot effect on playing.
A local tutor move needs an **advertised paid opening**, qualification fit, pickup and signed offer.

steps.text: Apply for advertised paid flute post if 2028 studio hours fall, education and pickup fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the orchestra that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to prove live music in a room matters. I would ask the studio to pay a senior teacher to watch my first group class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The advert recordings may end in 2031, but I could teach a paid group by then. Robots around 2034 could play a flute part onstage, though I do not know if families would want that at a concert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This autumn I would ask the studio to fund two observations with a senior teacher, with child pickup covered. If the teacher says I can manage six pupils, I would take a paid group only with preparation time and a staff member present; in the first year after 2031 I would keep it only while six pupils enroll and the hours fit home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until a group pays reliably. Five years gives me time to learn. A planned six-pupil flute class is not a fee until families pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept an unpaid teaching trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not run a class on an unpaid trial. The studio must put preparation hours in writing and pay the senior teacher to supervise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would school pickup fit a new class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner can take pickup on two afternoons, not every day. I would choose a class on one of those days rather than make the children wait.

I would defend **live orchestra music** in the five-year window.

feel: I feel **anxious** until the group produces reliable fees.
S3.quote: A planned six-pupil flute class is not a fee until families pay.
fieldNote: The group route needs **funded senior supervision** and approval before she teaches six pupils.
After 2031, paid preparation, **staff presence** and workable family pickup still matter.

steps.text: Observe senior teacher twice if studio funds it and child pickup is covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that AGI by 2036 gives us a decade to learn better ways to work. I would keep teaching real pupils while families pay for the studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 a paid group could replace my advert recordings, though it needs continued enrollment. Robots around 2039 may play onstage, but our current teaching and electrician income secure the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From this year I would save part of each paid recording fee after the mortgage and food clear, adding to our eight-month reserve. In the first year after 2036 I would compare actual studio and concert pay, and apply for an advertised school tutor post only if both shrink and its qualifications and pickup time fit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about later stage work. Our present household income and reserve make the near years manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would you try to save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would aim for twelve months of expenses by 2036 if recording jobs keep paying. I would not count an unpaid trial lesson toward savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What work lesson would you give your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My children should see that practice and a fair price belong together. I do not want my children working for praise when a bill needs money.

Keep **paid studio teaching** while families continue enrolling.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because recording fees could stop before studio hours are settled. A written timetable, an advertised qualified tutor role and paid group-training hours would give me useful options.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a child learns when a player listens back. My flute pupil hears a good phrase before knowing its name.

headlineQuote: My flute pupil hears a good phrase before knowing its name.
portrait: At **43**, Beth is a junior flutist with secondary school education, two children, a mortgage and eight months saved.
Her partner’s **electrician pay** steadies the household, while adverts and orchestra work add exposed fees.
She uses **AI daily** but tests new note checking with a nameless score, manual fingering and stop rule.
She seeks **funded group training** and qualified advertised posts, adding savings only from paid recordings after bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** may end advert recordings before Beth knows whether studio hours stay paid.
whatWouldHelp: A **written timetable**, qualified paid tutor opening and funded training would give Beth concrete choices.
